content: The essay states the conditions under which the equality holds. Ernie's argument is stipulated to include "all of the inferential steps that Ernie executed, and all of the support that Ernie took into account—citing any authorities that Ernie may have listened to himself." Fable's more realistic graph, in which the expert has seen evidence the listener has not, is the case the final paragraphs take up. Screening off in that case is partial, in proportion to the unseen evidence. Theorem plus concession yield a usable rule: authority's leftover weight scales with what the argument leaves out. Complete arguments are also received routinely where the essay's own erratum lives. A checked proof screens off its author, which is why mathematics refereeing works the same way for strangers and for Fields medallists.

quote: Assuming that Arthur is knowledgeable enough to understand all the technical arguments—otherwise they’re just impressive noises
content: The essay makes this point twice, the second time more strongly than Fable: "Otherwise, Ernie is simply uttering mystical syllables, and whether we 'believe' these syllables depends a great deal on his authority." So there is no dispute. For a listener who cannot evaluate the argument, authority carries the weight, and the essay says so. The theorem does not claim that everyone can check everything. It explains why the credential stops mattering once you can check. It is a reason to acquire the competence, not a license to pretend you have it. The Dunning-Kruger gloss in Fable's note is itself shakier than presented, since much of that pattern is regression and a better-than-average artifact (Krueger & Mueller 2002).

quote: But this slight strength of authority is only ceteris paribus, and can easily be overwhelmed by stronger arguments.
content: "Slight" follows from the theorem. Before you hear the argument, an expert's belief carries a large likelihood ratio, and the essay's opening scenario, 90% against 10% on assertion alone, grants that. Once the argument has been heard and checked, the likelihood ratio that remains is P(expert believes | argument, H) / P(expert believes | argument, ¬H). Screening off drives it toward one, and only the unseen-counterevidence term the essay names keeps it above one. The Jaynes example is framed as "the exact same statement" with the same argument, which is the residual case. The erratum shows the residual reaching zero where the argument is algebra. The adjective is the likelihood ratio, evaluated after the argument has been heard.
